cards.explanation: The answer is tear his prey. The lament says, “After learning to tear his prey…” and then it tells where that leads. Some folks learn to cook. This young lion learned something a lot rougher. Keep your eye on him, friends, because the nations are paying attention too. (Ezekiel 19:3)

The answer is that he's trapped in their pit. The lament says, “When the nations heard of him, he was trapped in their pit.” Word got around about this lion, and the nations had a pit ready. Nobody here is handing out a welcome basket. Then they lead him off with hooks to Egypt. (Ezekiel 19:4)

The answer is True. The text says that when she saw she had waited in vain and her hope was lost, she took another of her cubs and made him a young lion. So the lament doesn't stop at one cub. She tries again with another. Hang on to that, friends, because this second cub gets a whole stretch of the lament to himself. (Ezekiel 19:5)

The word is devastates. The lament says, “He broke down their strongholds and devastated their cities.” Strongholds are fortified places, and he breaks them down. This is a lion who doesn't knock before he enters. And the whole land notices. (Ezekiel 19:7)

The answer is a net, friends. The text says the nations “…spread their net over him; he was trapped in their pit.” They came from the provinces on every side, so this was no lone hunter. Roar all you want, a net doesn't care. It's a net-and-pit combo. (Ezekiel 19:8)

The answer is the king of Babylon. The lament says, “With hooks they caged him and brought him to the king of Babylon.” So this time it's the king of Babylon, not Egypt like the first cub. Hooks and a cage. It's a rough ride for a lion. (Ezekiel 19:9)

The answer is False. The lament says he was taken into captivity so that his roar was “…heard no longer on the mountains of Israel.” The same roar that made the land shudder has gone silent there. That's a big change for a lion who once filled the whole place with noise. (Ezekiel 19:9)

The answer is fruitful and full of branches. The lament says the vine “…was fruitful and full of branches because of the abundant waters.” It's planted by the water, and it shows. Think of a plant that gets everything it needs and just goes for it. (Ezekiel 19:10)

The answer is False, friends. The lament says the vine towered high above the thick branches. It was conspicuous for its height and for its dense foliage. This one is standing out, not staying low. (Ezekiel 19:11)

The answer is the east wind dries it up. The lament says the vine was uprooted in fury and cast down to the ground, and “…the east wind dried up its fruit.” So the wind is what dries the fruit. It's like a batch left on the counter with the oven off and the window open all week. No one's eating that one. (Ezekiel 19:12)

The answer is True. The lament says the vine's strong branches were stripped off and they withered, and then, “the fire consumed them.” First they dry out, then the fire finishes the job. It's a hard picture, friends, and I think it's meant to be. (Ezekiel 19:12)

The answer is in the wilderness. The lament says, “Now it is planted in the wilderness, in a dry and thirsty land.” Remember where it started: planted by abundant waters. Now it's a dry and thirsty land. That's a long way from the water. (Ezekiel 19:13)

The answer is its fruit. The lament says, “Fire has gone out from its main branch and devoured its fruit…” The fire starts at the main branch and the fruit goes with it. It's a rough ending for a vine that began so fruitful. (Ezekiel 19:14)
